newsitem.title: USA: Prosecutors stress human tragedy of Oklahoma blast.
newsitem.headline: Prosecutors stress human tragedy of Oklahoma blast.

text.p: Prosecutors in the Oklahoma City bombing trial drove home the human tragedy of the blast as they built up to the end of their case on Wednesday, presenting emotional testimony from a survivor and a rescue worker.

The prosecution was expected to rest its case later on Wednesday after weaving a web of circumstantial evidence against Timothy McVeigh, who is accused of blowing up the Alfred P. Murrah federal building on April 19, 1995, killing 168 people in the worst attack on civilians in U.S. history.
Late on Wednesday morning, the prosecution called what it said would be its final witness, Fred Jordan, chief medical examiner for the state of Oklahoma who identified many of the bombing victims.

The prosecution has presented more than 130 witnesses in 18 days, moving far more quickly than expected. Chief defence attorney Stephen Jones said he expected to put his first witness on the stand on Thursday.

The prosecution returned to its starting point, seeking to leave jurors with the panic and horror felt by survivors and rescue workers as they realised the magnitude of the death and destruction in the minutes after the bombing.

Florence Rogers, chief executive of the Federal Employees Credit Union which was on the third floor of the Oklahoma City federal building, described in a low voice how seven women employees she was holding a meeting with in her office were blown away by the blast.
"I leaned back in my chair when literally the whole building started to blow up. I was thrown against the floor in kind of a tornado-like rush," Rogers testified.

"When I was able to stand up, all of the girls in my office had totally disappeared, with the six floors up above us on top of them. I never saw them again," she said, her low monotone enhancing the power of her story.

Rogers gravely read out the names of the 18 employees of the credit union who were killed in the blast and pointed out on a floor plan where they were when she last saw them. One woman employee had worked for the credit union just eight days and another woman was seven months pregnant, she said.
Just 18 inches (one half metre) from Rogers' desk, there was a gaping hole where part of the building had been blown away, she said.
Relatives of bombing victims sobbed in court as Rogers gave the names of the victims. The credit union, a kind of bank, is not a federal agency.

The government says McVeigh, a 29-year-old Gulf War veteran, bombed the federal building to avenge the deaths of 80 Branch Davidian cult members in a clash with federal agents at Waco, Texas, exactly two years before the bombing. He has pleaded not guilty but could face the death penalty if convicted.

Mike Shannon, special operations chief of the Oklahoma City Fire Department and one of the first rescuers in the building, told how a bomb scare forced rescuers to leave the building 90 minutes after the blast, leaving four or five survivors trapped inside.

The bomb scare was caused by a desk clock shaped like a "TV comic strip bomb", he said. Someone spotted the clock -- belonging to an agent of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms -- which had been knocked into the stairwell, and raised the alarm. People were very nervous at the time, fearing there could be a second explosion.

Shannon, wearing his fire department uniform, described his dilemma as he decided to evacuate the building, torn between his duty to help survivors and his responsibility not to endanger rescue workers. Rescue workers begged and pleaded to be allowed a few more minutes to rescue the people they were helping, he said.
Nine floors of the building collapsed, creating a pile of rubble that reached the third floor and covered 7,000 square feet (650 square metres), he said.
Blood and gore from the dead coated rescuers' helmets, posing a biological hazard, Shannon said in his graphic testimony. Falling debris posed another threat.
At times, Shannon's testimony seemed to become too graphic for federal Judge Richard Matsch, who sharply asked prosecutors what his testimony proved.
